\section[il romanziere]{il romanziere — novelist}

\label{lesson:IT-C524-romanziere}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for fresco, then the Italian for to restore.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: il romanziere}
\textbf{il romanziere} — \textquotedblleft{}novelist\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Il romanziere presenta il suo nuovo libro in libreria.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The novelist is presenting his new book in the bookshop.}
\end{quote}

A woman is \emph{la romanziera}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{romanziere} is built on \emph{romanzo} \textquotedblleft{}novel\textquotedblright{}, from Old French \emph{romanz} \textquotedblleft{}a story told in the common tongue\textquotedblright{}, from Vulgar Latin \emph{rōmānicē} \textquotedblleft{}in the Roman manner\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il romanziere}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il romanziere}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{il romanziere}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for fresco, then the Italian for to restore, then say \emph{il romanziere} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does il romanziere mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Novelist\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[il capitolo]{il capitolo — chapter}

\label{lesson:IT-C524-capitolo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to restore, then the Italian for novelist.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: il capitolo}
\textbf{il capitolo} — \textquotedblleft{}chapter\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Leggo un capitolo ogni sera prima di dormire.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I read a chapter every evening before I go to sleep.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Nel prossimo capitolo} — in the next chapter.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{capitolo} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{capitulum} \textquotedblleft{}a little head, a heading\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from \emph{caput} \textquotedblleft{}head\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il capitolo}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il capitolo}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{il capitolo}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for to restore, then the Italian for novelist, then say \emph{il capitolo} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[ambientare]{ambientare — to set (a story)}

\label{lesson:IT-C524-ambientare}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for novelist, then the Italian for chapter.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ambientare}
\textbf{ambientare} — \textquotedblleft{}to set (a story)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Il romanzo è ambientato in un piccolo paese di montagna.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The novel is set in a small mountain village.}
\end{quote}

Mostly \emph{essere ambientato} — to be set (in).

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ambientare} is built on \emph{ambiente} \textquotedblleft{}surroundings\textquotedblright{}, a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{ambiēns} \textquotedblleft{}going round\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{ambīre}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ambientare}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ambientare}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{ambientare}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for novelist, then the Italian for chapter, then say \emph{ambientare} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does ambientare mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To set (a story)\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[il colpo di scena]{il colpo di scena — twist (in a story)}

\label{lesson:IT-C524-colpo-di-scena}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for chapter, then the Italian for to set.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: il colpo di scena}
\textbf{il colpo di scena} — \textquotedblleft{}twist (in a story)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Alla fine c'è un colpo di scena incredibile.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{At the end there is an incredible twist.}
\end{quote}

Literally \textquotedblleft{}a blow of the stage\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{colpo di scena} is built from \emph{colpo} \textquotedblleft{}blow\textquotedblright{}, inherited from Vulgar Latin \emph{colpus}, from Latin \emph{colaphus} \textquotedblleft{}a punch\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), and \emph{scena} \textquotedblleft{}scene\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{scaena}, from Greek \emph{skēn\'{\={e}}} \textquotedblleft{}a stage\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il colpo di scena}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il colpo di scena}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{il colpo di scena}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for chapter, then the Italian for to set, then say \emph{il colpo di scena} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]

\section[l'epilogo]{l'epilogo — ending, epilogue}

\label{lesson:IT-C524-epilogo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to set, then the Italian for twist.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: l'epilogo}
\textbf{l'epilogo} — \textquotedblleft{}ending, epilogue\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
L'epilogo del libro mi ha sorpreso.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The ending of the book surprised me.}
\end{quote}

Also the end of a real story: \emph{l'epilogo della vicenda}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{epilogo} is a learned borrowing, through Latin \emph{epilogus}, from Greek \emph{epílogos} \textquotedblleft{}a conclusion\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB, under English \emph{epilogue}), from \emph{légein} \textquotedblleft{}to speak\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{l'epilogo}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{l'epilogo}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{l'epilogo}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for to set, then the Italian for twist, then say \emph{l'epilogo} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
